date.label: Undated thematic Leviticus legislation
date.note: This is a literary and thematic grouping in the Sinai narrative, not an independent datable event. No absolute year is inferred.

claims.claim: Leviticus 11 distinguishes edible animals from prohibited animals and addresses impurity from carcasses.
Leviticus 12 specifies a period and concluding offering following childbirth.
claims.evidence: Lev 12:1–8; childbirth does not imply a moral fault in the mother.

claims.claim: Leviticus 13–14 assigns priests responsibility to inspect and pronounce the ritual status of affected people and materials.
Leviticus 15 differentiates ordinary emissions and menstruation from other discharges and prescribes purification measures.
The affliction called ṣāraʿat should not be identified without qualification with modern Hansen’s disease; Leviticus uses the term for conditions affecting skin, textiles, and houses.
claims.evidence: Lev 13–14 (KJV, inspected); Baden and Moss, JBL 130(4) 2011 pp. 643–662 full scholarly article inspected; the term covers people and also clothes/houses, so do not equate it unqualifiedly with a modern bacterial diagnosis.

claims.claim: Ritual impurity is not automatically equivalent to moral sin in this legislation.
claims.evidence: Lev 12 and 15 (KJV, inspected), including childbirth and normal emissions; Baden and Moss 2011 full pp. 643–662 distinguish Priestly ṣāraʿat legislation from some punitive biblical narratives. Do not infer all impure persons were culpable.

claims.claim: Explanations of food classifications as hygiene, symbol, identity, or ecology are competing modern reconstructions.
claims.evidence: Lev 11 (KJV); Hawley, CBQ 77(2) 2015 pp. 231–249, author-hosted full article read; surveys differing animal-taxonomy explanations and offers one Priestly literary/theological model, not a universal explanation or ancient health department.

claims.claim: Purity rules are related to ordered access to sacred space and the divine dwelling.
claims.evidence: Lev 15:31 (KJV chapter directly inspected) associates impurity practices with the tabernacle among the people; this is scriptural textual evidence only.

connections.note: A related dietary inventory permits direct comparison between the legal corpora.
Camp exclusion applies to specified impurity conditions.
Miriam’s skin condition is narrated separately; its cause must not be universalized to Leviticus.
Naaman’s account portrays a distinct narrative treatment of a skin condition.
Luke explicitly refers to purification and a prescribed offering after Jesus’s birth.
Jesus and the Pharisees dispute handwashing and defilement in a later setting.
Peter’s vision later draws on clean/unclean imagery without being a simple historical exposition of Leviticus.
Hebrews repurposes ritual purification language in Christian theological interpretation.
